text: The four Bell states are the maximally entangled basis for two qubits — states you'll see constructed, measured, and referenced constantly for the rest of this course. This lesson builds one with real gates and shows exactly what measuring it gives you.

Starting from the four two-qubit basis states, you get four Bell states: Phi-plus, ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2; Phi-minus, the same with a minus sign; Psi-plus, ket-01 plus ket-10 over root 2; and Psi-minus, that pair with a minus sign. Each is entangled by exactly the same non-factorizability argument from last lesson, and together they form the Bell basis — a complete alternative to the computational basis for two qubits.

Here's the standard recipe, starting from ket-00. First, Hadamard on qubit 1 only: the state becomes ket-00 plus ket-10, over root 2 — still a product state, no entanglement yet. Second, CNOT with qubit 1 as control and qubit 2 as target: the ket-00 term's control is 0, so the target is untouched; the ket-10 term's control is 1, so the target flips, turning it into ket-11. Putting the terms back together gives ket-00 plus ket-11 over root 2 — exactly Phi-plus.

Measure qubit 1 of Phi-plus in the computational basis. By the Born rule, the probability of each outcome is 0.5, and in that branch the state is exactly ket-00 or exactly ket-11. So qubit 1 alone is a perfect coin flip — nothing special there. The remarkable part is the relationship: once you learn qubit 1's result, qubit 2's result is no longer a probability at all, it's certain. P of 00 and P of 11 are each 0.5; P of 01 and P of 10 are exactly zero.

The four Bell states aren't just examples of entanglement — they're the extremal case. No two-qubit state can produce stronger per-measurement correlation than a Bell state does, which is exactly why they're the default building block anywhere two qubits need to be linked. Teleportation and superdense coding, coming in chapter 5, both start by preparing a Bell pair exactly the way this lesson just built one.
Next lesson takes seriously the most common objection: isn't this just two coins secretly prepared to match? We'll show exactly where that explanation works, and exactly where it runs out of road.
